lesson.title: The Equivalence Point: Where the Math Meets the Curve
lesson.summary: The equivalence point is the exact volume of titrant at which the moles added are stoichiometrically equivalent to the moles of analyte originally present, and it appears on a titration curve as the steepest point of the graph.
lesson.body:
The equivalence point is a precise, calculable moment: it is the volume of titrant at which the titrant added has exactly reacted with all of the analyte, according to the mole ratio in the balanced equation. It is worth being exact about that last phrase, because equivalence point is not defined by equal volumes and it is not defined by equal moles either, unless the reaction happens to be a 1 to 1 ratio. It is defined by stoichiometric equivalence, whatever ratio the balanced equation actually specifies.

On a titration curve, the equivalence point sits at the steepest part of the S-shaped curve, the inflection point where the graph transitions from rising slowly to rising steeply and back to rising slowly again. That steep jump happens because, right at stoichiometric equivalence, there is essentially no leftover analyte left to resist further pH change, so even a tiny additional volume of titrant swings the pH dramatically.

For a reaction with a 1 to 1 mole ratio, like the HCl and NaOH titration from earlier chapters, the equivalence point volume can be found directly from M1V1 = M2V2. But many important titrations do not have a 1 to 1 ratio, and those cases show clearly why equivalence point is a stoichiometric idea, not a simple volume-matching one. Consider titrating 25.00 mL of 0.200 M sulfuric acid, H2SO4, with 0.250 M NaOH, following the reaction H2SO4 + 2NaOH -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O. First find moles of H2SO4: 0.02500 L times 0.200 mol/L equals 0.00500 mol, or 5.00 mmol. The balanced equation requires 2 mol of NaOH for every 1 mol of H2SO4, so the moles of NaOH needed at equivalence is 2 times 5.00 mmol, which equals 10.0 mmol. Solving for volume, 10.0 mmol divided by 0.250 mol/L equals 40.0 mL. The equivalence point for this titration occurs at 40.0 mL of NaOH added, noticeably more than the 25.00 mL of acid you started with, precisely because each mole of this acid demands two moles of base.

Diprotic and triprotic acids like H2SO4 can, under the right conditions, show more than one equivalence point on a single curve, one for each proton being neutralized in sequence, though the two equivalence points are not always distinct enough to resolve clearly on a real graph. The broader point to take forward is that equivalence point is a calculated, theoretical location. In an actual titration, a chemist cannot see pH directly mid-experiment without an instrument, so they rely on a color-changing indicator to signal when the reaction looks complete, and choosing the right indicator so that its visible signal lines up with the true, calculated equivalence point is the whole challenge of indicator selection, taken up next.
